tags.name: SaaS transfers all responsibility
tags.description: Believes that using SaaS means the provider is responsible for everything, including the customer's data and identities.
tags.correct_concept: Data, devices, and accounts/identities are always the customer's responsibility, in every service type.

tags.name: Over-assigns infrastructure to customer
tags.description: Believes the customer manages physical hosts, datacenters, or provider-side infrastructure.
tags.correct_concept: Physical hosts, network, and datacenter are always the provider's responsibility in the public cloud.

tags.name: PaaS customer patches platform
tags.description: Believes a PaaS customer still patches the database engine, runtime, or underlying OS.
tags.correct_concept: In PaaS the provider manages the OS and platform runtime; the customer manages data, access, and application configuration.

tags.name: Provider patches IaaS guest OS
tags.description: Believes Microsoft patches and manages the guest OS of an IaaS virtual machine automatically.
tags.correct_concept: In IaaS the customer manages the guest OS, including patching; the provider manages the physical layer and hypervisor.

tags.name: Shared means 50/50
tags.description: Reads 'shared responsibility' as an equal split of every task.
tags.correct_concept: Responsibility is divided by layer and service type, not split equally task by task.

tags.name: Reverses CapEx and OpEx
tags.description: Swaps capital expenditure (upfront purchase) and operational expenditure (ongoing spend).
tags.correct_concept: Cloud moves spend from CapEx (buying hardware upfront) to OpEx (paying as you consume).

tags.name: Cloud pricing is fixed
tags.description: Believes cloud costs are fixed or unrelated to usage under the consumption-based model.
tags.correct_concept: The consumption-based model bills for what you use, with no upfront capital cost.

tags.name: Elasticity confused with availability
tags.description: Confuses automatic scaling (elasticity) with high availability or uptime.
tags.correct_concept: Elasticity adjusts resources to demand; high availability keeps services accessible despite failures.

tags.name: Mixes up cloud benefit terms
tags.description: Confuses cloud benefits such as predictability, agility, or geo-distribution with the scenario described.
tags.correct_concept: Match the scenario to the benefit: elasticity = auto scale to demand; agility = fast provisioning; predictability = performance and cost forecasting.

tags.name: Mixes up public/private/hybrid
tags.description: Confuses public, private, and hybrid cloud definitions.
tags.correct_concept: Hybrid combines on-premises (or private) with public cloud, letting data stay on-premises while workloads burst to Azure.

tags.name: Multicloud means hybrid
tags.description: Treats multicloud (several cloud providers) as the same as hybrid (on-premises plus cloud).
tags.correct_concept: Multicloud = more than one cloud provider; hybrid = on-premises plus cloud.

tags.name: Mixes up IaaS/PaaS/SaaS
tags.description: Confuses the three service types, e.g. treats any hosted app as SaaS or any hosted workload as IaaS.
tags.correct_concept: IaaS = you manage OS and up; PaaS = you manage app and data; SaaS = you consume finished software.

tags.name: Practice vs service model
tags.description: Confuses a practice (such as infrastructure as code) with a cloud service model.
tags.correct_concept: IaaS/PaaS/SaaS describe who manages what; IaC is a way of deploying resources.

tags.name: High availability vs disaster recovery
tags.description: Confuses staying available through component failures (HA) with recovering after a major outage (DR).
tags.correct_concept: HA minimises downtime during failures; DR restores service after a major disruption.

tags.name: Scale up vs scale out
tags.description: Confuses vertical scaling (bigger instance) with horizontal scaling (more instances).
tags.correct_concept: Scaling out/horizontal adds instances; scaling up/vertical makes one instance larger.

tags.name: Scaling vs resilience or cost
tags.description: Confuses scaling with failover or cost optimisation.
tags.correct_concept: Scaling changes capacity for load; failover and right-sizing address resilience and cost.

tags.name: Region pair vs availability zone
tags.description: Confuses region pairs (disaster recovery across regions) with availability zones (datacenters within one region).
tags.correct_concept: Availability zones protect against datacenter failure; region pairs support recovery from a regional disaster.

tags.name: Misdefines availability zones
tags.description: Believes availability zones share power, cooling, or networking.
tags.correct_concept: Each availability zone has independent power, cooling, and networking.

tags.name: Management group / subscription order
tags.description: Reverses the order of management groups and subscriptions.
tags.correct_concept: Hierarchy: management group > subscription > resource group > resource.

tags.name: Resource group above subscription
tags.description: Believes resource groups sit above subscriptions.
tags.correct_concept: Resource groups live inside a subscription and hold resources.

tags.name: Deleting a resource group keeps resources
tags.description: Believes resources survive deletion of their resource group.
tags.correct_concept: Deleting a resource group deletes every resource in it.

tags.name: Subscription treated as regional construct
tags.description: Confuses subscriptions (billing/access boundary) with regional or resiliency constructs.
tags.correct_concept: A subscription is a billing and access boundary, not a resiliency feature.

tags.name: Over-scopes deletion
tags.description: Believes deleting a resource group deletes the subscription.
tags.correct_concept: Deletion cascades downward (group to resources), not upward.

tags.name: Defaults to VMs for everything
tags.description: Chooses virtual machines (IaaS) for workloads suited to higher-level services.
tags.correct_concept: Match the compute option to the need: VMs for control, containers, serverless for event-driven code.

tags.name: AKS vs simple containers
tags.description: Chooses AKS when a single containerised app needs no orchestration, or confuses it with serverless.
tags.correct_concept: AKS is for orchestrated container workloads; Azure Container Instances runs single containers on demand.

tags.name: Desktop virtualisation confusion
tags.description: Confuses Azure Virtual Desktop with application or container hosting.
tags.correct_concept: Azure Virtual Desktop delivers desktops and apps to users; it does not host containers.

tags.name: App Service vs Functions
tags.description: Confuses always-on web hosting (App Service) with event-driven, per-execution serverless (Functions).
tags.correct_concept: Azure Functions runs code in response to events and bills per execution.

tags.name: LRS protects against datacenter loss
tags.description: Believes locally redundant storage survives a datacenter failure.
tags.correct_concept: LRS keeps three copies inside a single datacenter; ZRS spreads across availability zones.

tags.name: ZRS vs GRS
tags.description: Confuses zone redundancy (same region) with geo-redundancy (secondary region, asynchronous).
tags.correct_concept: ZRS = synchronous across zones in one region; GRS = asynchronous copy to a paired region.

tags.name: Access tier vs redundancy
tags.description: Confuses access tiers (hot/cool/archive) with redundancy options.
tags.correct_concept: Access tiers control cost versus access speed; redundancy controls data copies.

tags.name: Blob vs Azure Files
tags.description: Confuses object storage (Blob) with SMB/NFS file shares (Azure Files).
tags.correct_concept: Blob storage holds unstructured objects such as images and video.

tags.name: Blob vs Table
tags.description: Confuses object storage with NoSQL key-value (Table) storage.
tags.correct_concept: Table storage holds structured NoSQL data, not media objects.

tags.name: Blob vs Queue
tags.description: Confuses object storage with message queuing.
tags.correct_concept: Queue storage holds messages for asynchronous processing.

tags.name: VPN Gateway vs ExpressRoute
tags.description: Believes a VPN Gateway is a private connection that avoids the public internet.
tags.correct_concept: VPN Gateway sends encrypted traffic over the public internet; ExpressRoute is a private connection.

tags.name: Bastion vs connectivity
tags.description: Confuses Azure Bastion (secure RDP/SSH to VMs) with site-to-cloud connectivity.
tags.correct_concept: Bastion gives secure browser-based RDP/SSH to VMs; it is not a hybrid network link.

tags.name: VNet peering vs on-premises link
tags.description: Confuses virtual network peering with connecting on-premises networks.
tags.correct_concept: Peering connects Azure virtual networks to each other.

tags.name: NSG vs Azure Firewall
tags.description: Confuses basic NSG rules with the centralised, managed Azure Firewall service.
tags.correct_concept: NSGs filter traffic by 5-tuple rules on subnets or NICs; Azure Firewall is a managed, centralised network security service.

tags.name: Load balancing vs filtering
tags.description: Believes a load balancer filters traffic.
tags.correct_concept: Load Balancer distributes traffic; it does not apply allow/deny security rules.

tags.name: DNS vs filtering
tags.description: Believes Azure DNS controls traffic flow.
tags.correct_concept: Azure DNS resolves names; it does not filter traffic.

tags.name: Entra ID is AD DS
tags.description: Believes Microsoft Entra ID supports LDAP, Kerberos, and domain join like on-premises AD DS.
tags.correct_concept: Entra Domain Services provides managed domain services (LDAP, Kerberos, NTLM, domain join).

tags.name: Permissions vs directory services
tags.description: Confuses authorization/permission features with directory services.
tags.correct_concept: RBAC grants permissions on Azure resources; it provides no directory or domain services.

tags.name: Authentication vs authorization
tags.description: Swaps authentication (proving identity) and authorization (what you can access).
tags.correct_concept: Authentication verifies who you are; authorization decides what you can do.

tags.name: SSO vs authentication
tags.description: Treats single sign-on as the act of verifying identity.
tags.correct_concept: SSO lets one sign-in reach many apps; the verification step is authentication.

tags.name: RBAC vs Conditional Access
tags.description: Confuses permissions on resources (RBAC) with sign-in controls (Conditional Access).
tags.correct_concept: Conditional Access enforces controls such as MFA at sign-in based on signals; RBAC grants access to resources.

tags.name: Azure Policy vs RBAC
tags.description: Confuses rules on what can be deployed (Policy) with who may act (RBAC).
tags.correct_concept: Policy enforces resource configuration standards; RBAC controls who can do what.

tags.name: Policy vs locks vs other governance
tags.description: Confuses locks (prevent change/delete) with Policy or with cost/optimisation tools.
tags.correct_concept: Locks block accidental deletion or modification; Policy governs configuration.

tags.name: Policy prevents deletion
tags.description: Believes Azure Policy protects existing resources from deletion.
tags.correct_concept: Use a CanNotDelete lock to prevent deletion; Policy evaluates configuration and compliance.

tags.name: Tags enforce rules
tags.description: Believes tags enforce behaviour.
tags.correct_concept: Tags are metadata for organising and cost reporting; they do not enforce controls.

tags.name: RBAC scope not inherited
tags.description: Believes a role assigned at a higher scope applies only to that scope object.
tags.correct_concept: RBAC permissions are inherited by child scopes: management group, subscription, resource group, resource.

tags.name: RBAC applies only to new resources
tags.description: Believes role assignments cover only resources created afterward.
tags.correct_concept: Role assignments apply to existing and future resources within the scope.

tags.name: RBAC prevents deletion by Owners
tags.description: Uses permissions to stop accidental deletion instead of a lock.
tags.correct_concept: Locks override user permissions, including Owner.

tags.name: TCO vs Pricing calculator
tags.description: Confuses the TCO calculator (on-premises vs Azure comparison) with the Pricing calculator (cost of Azure resources).
tags.correct_concept: Pricing calculator estimates Azure costs; TCO calculator compares on-premises costs with Azure.

tags.name: Cost Management vs estimation
tags.description: Confuses Cost Management (analyse actual spend) with pre-deployment estimation.
tags.correct_concept: Cost Management analyses and budgets actual spend.

tags.name: Tags reduce cost
tags.description: Believes tagging itself lowers cost.
tags.correct_concept: Tags help allocate and report costs; reservations or right-sizing reduce them.

tags.name: Grouping gives discounts
tags.description: Believes management groups or similar structures provide pricing discounts.
tags.correct_concept: Management groups organise governance; they do not discount prices.

tags.name: Composite SLA is the highest
tags.description: Picks the higher of the individual SLAs.
tags.correct_concept: Composite SLA is the product of the dependent services' SLAs, so it is lower than each.

tags.name: Composite SLA is the average
tags.description: Averages the individual SLAs.
tags.correct_concept: Multiply the SLAs rather than averaging them.

tags.name: Composite SLA reaches 100%
tags.description: Believes combining services yields 100% availability.
tags.correct_concept: Chained dependencies lower the combined SLA; redundancy is needed to raise it.

tags.name: Monitor vs Service Health
tags.description: Confuses Azure Monitor (your resources' telemetry) with Service Health (Azure platform incidents).
tags.correct_concept: Service Health reports Azure outages and maintenance affecting you; Monitor collects metrics and logs.

tags.name: Advisor vs other tools
tags.description: Confuses Azure Advisor recommendations with monitoring, health, or security services.
tags.correct_concept: Advisor gives personalised best-practice recommendations; it does not report incidents or enforce security.

tags.name: Defender for Cloud vs identity controls
tags.description: Confuses Defender for Cloud (posture and threat protection) with identity services.
tags.correct_concept: Defender for Cloud assesses security posture and protects workloads; it does not control sign-in.

tags.name: Identity service vs posture management
tags.description: Believes Microsoft Entra ID provides workload security posture management.
tags.correct_concept: Entra ID is identity; Defender for Cloud handles workload security posture.

tags.name: Mixes up management interfaces
tags.description: Confuses graphical (portal) and command-line interfaces.
tags.correct_concept: Portal is a web GUI; CLI and PowerShell are command line; Cloud Shell is a browser-based shell.

tags.name: Templates vs shells
tags.description: Confuses declarative templates with interactive shells.
tags.correct_concept: ARM/Bicep templates declare resources; shells run commands.

tags.name: Arc vs IaC
tags.description: Believes Azure Arc is used to deploy repeatable environments.
tags.correct_concept: Azure Arc extends Azure management to resources outside Azure; it is not a templating tool.

tags.name: Local module vs browser shell
tags.description: Believes PowerShell always needs local installation.
tags.correct_concept: Cloud Shell offers a pre-authenticated browser-based environment with Azure CLI and PowerShell.

tags.name: Shell vs declarative deployment
tags.description: Believes Cloud Shell is a declarative deployment method.
tags.correct_concept: Cloud Shell is where you run commands; ARM/Bicep declares the desired state.

tags.name: Portal deployments are repeatable
tags.description: Believes manual portal clicks give repeatable, consistent deployments.
tags.correct_concept: Infrastructure as code (ARM templates, Bicep) provides repeatable, consistent deployments.

questions.stem: A manager says: "We use Microsoft 365 (SaaS), so Microsoft is responsible for everything." Which item is still always the company's responsibility?

options.rationale: Data, devices, and accounts/identities remain the customer's responsibility in every service type.
Physical security is always the cloud provider's responsibility.

options.text: Patching the host servers' operating system
options.rationale: Host infrastructure is managed by the provider in SaaS.

options.text: Nothing, because SaaS transfers all responsibility to the provider
options.rationale: Even in SaaS the customer remains responsible for data, devices, and identities.

questions.explanation: Under the shared responsibility model, the customer always owns their information and data, devices, and accounts and identities. Physical infrastructure always belongs to the provider; OS and application layers shift to the provider as you move from IaaS to PaaS to SaaS.
questions.concept_note: Always the customer: information and data, devices, accounts and identities. Always the provider: physical datacenter, network, and hosts.

questions.stem: A company runs a Windows Server virtual machine in Azure (IaaS). Who is responsible for managing and patching the guest operating system?

options.text: Microsoft, because Azure hosts the virtual machine
options.rationale: Hosting the VM does not make Microsoft responsible for the guest OS.
In IaaS the customer manages the guest OS (and everything above it); Microsoft manages the physical hosts and hypervisor.

options.text: Responsibility is split 50/50, with each side patching half of the OS
options.rationale: Responsibility is divided by layer, not split evenly.

options.text: Azure always patches every VM automatically, so nobody needs to act
options.rationale: Patching is not automatic by default; the customer is responsible for guest OS management.

questions.explanation: In IaaS, the provider is responsible for the physical datacenter, network, and hosts, while the customer manages the operating system, applications, and data on the VM.
questions.concept_note: IaaS: customer manages OS, runtime, apps, data. Provider manages physical hosts, network, datacenter.

questions.stem: A company stops buying servers upfront and instead pays monthly for the Azure resources it uses. How does this change its spending?

options.text: It shifts spending from operational expenditure to capital expenditure
options.rationale: This reverses the terms.

options.text: Costs become fixed and no longer depend on usage
options.rationale: The consumption-based model ties cost to usage.

options.text: It shifts spending from capital expenditure to operational expenditure
options.rationale: Upfront hardware purchases (CapEx) are replaced by ongoing, usage-based costs (OpEx).

options.text: Costs are unchanged because Azure bills once per year
options.rationale: Azure bills based on usage, typically monthly.

questions.explanation: Cloud shifts spending from CapEx (buying hardware upfront) to OpEx (paying for what you use). The consumption-based model means no upfront cost and you pay only for resources consumed.
questions.concept_note: CapEx = upfront purchase. OpEx = ongoing spend. Consumption-based = pay for what you use.

questions.stem: An online shop's traffic spikes during sales. Its Azure resources automatically scale out during the spike and scale back in afterwards. Which cloud benefit is this?

options.rationale: High availability is about staying accessible despite failures.
Predictability is about forecasting performance and cost.
Geo-distribution is about placing services near users worldwide.
Elasticity automatically adjusts resources to match demand.

questions.explanation: Elasticity is the ability to add and remove resources automatically as demand changes, so you pay only for what is needed.
questions.concept_note: Elasticity = automatic scale out and in to match demand.

questions.stem: A company must keep sensitive data in its own datacenter but wants to use Azure for extra capacity during busy periods. Which cloud model fits?

options.rationale: Hybrid combines on-premises infrastructure with public cloud.
A pure public cloud would place all resources in the provider's datacenters.
A private cloud alone does not use Azure's public capacity.
Multicloud means using more than one cloud provider, not combining on-premises with cloud.

questions.explanation: A hybrid cloud combines on-premises (or private cloud) resources with public cloud, allowing sensitive data to stay on-premises while workloads burst into Azure.
questions.concept_note: Public = provider datacenters. Private = organisation-owned. Hybrid = both. Multicloud = multiple providers.

questions.stem: A developer wants to publish a web app without managing the operating system or web server runtime. Which service type does this describe?

options.rationale: In IaaS you manage the OS and runtime.
PaaS (for example Azure App Service) lets you deploy code while the provider manages OS and runtime.
SaaS is finished software you consume, not a platform to run your own app.
IaC is a deployment practice, not a service model.

questions.explanation: PaaS provides a managed platform for building and running applications without managing underlying OS or runtime.
questions.concept_note: PaaS: customer manages app and data; provider manages OS, runtime, and infrastructure.

questions.stem: The architecture team wants an application to stay accessible with minimal downtime when individual hardware components fail. Which principle does this describe?

options.rationale: Disaster recovery is about restoring service after a major disruption.
Elasticity adjusts capacity to demand.
High availability keeps services accessible with minimal downtime during failures.
Agility is about quickly provisioning and changing resources.

questions.explanation: High availability is designed so workloads continue running with minimal interruption when components fail. Disaster recovery addresses recovery from larger-scale outages.
questions.concept_note: HA = minimal downtime through component failures. DR = recover after major disruption.

questions.stem: A company uses Azure SQL Database (PaaS). Which task remains the company's responsibility?

options.text: Applying patches to the database engine
options.rationale: In PaaS the provider patches the database engine.

options.text: Maintaining the operating system of the underlying servers
options.rationale: The provider manages the OS in PaaS.

options.text: Maintaining the physical network in the datacenter
options.rationale: Physical network is always the provider's responsibility.

options.text: Managing which accounts and identities can access the data
options.rationale: Accounts, identities, and data are always the customer's responsibility.

questions.explanation: In PaaS the provider manages the platform (OS, engine patches, physical layers); the customer still manages data and identities/access.
questions.concept_note: PaaS: provider manages OS and platform runtime. Customer manages data, identities, and application configuration.

questions.stem: Traffic to an app increases, so you add more virtual machine instances behind a load balancer. What is this called?

options.rationale: Adding more instances is scaling out.
Scaling up makes one instance bigger.
Failover switches to a standby after a failure.
Right-sizing adjusts resources to reduce cost.

questions.explanation: Scaling out (horizontal) adds more instances; scaling up (vertical) adds CPU or memory to an existing instance.
questions.concept_note: Out/horizontal = more instances. Up/vertical = larger instance.

questions.stem: You need a VM workload to remain available if one datacenter in an Azure region fails. What should you use?

options.rationale: Region pairs address large-scale regional disasters.
Availability zones are physically separate datacenters within a region, with independent power, cooling, and networking.
A resource group is a logical container with no resiliency function.
Management groups organise subscriptions; they do not affect availability.

questions.explanation: Deploying across availability zones protects against a datacenter-level failure within a region.
questions.concept_note: Availability zone = separate datacenters in one region. Region pair = two regions in the same geography.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes an Azure region pair?

options.text: Two datacenters inside the same Azure region
options.rationale: That describes availability zones.

options.text: Two subscriptions linked for shared billing
options.rationale: Subscriptions are not geographic constructs.

options.text: Two regions in the same geography, paired to support disaster recovery
options.rationale: Region pairs support recovery from regional disasters.

options.text: Two availability zones that share the same power source
options.rationale: Availability zones have independent power.

questions.explanation: Each region is paired with another in the same geography to support disaster recovery and coordinated platform updates.
questions.concept_note: Region pair = two regions, same geography, for disaster recovery.

questions.stem: Which option shows Azure's resource hierarchy from the top level down?

options.text: Subscription, management group, resource group, resource
options.rationale: Management groups sit above subscriptions.

options.text: Management group, resource group, subscription, resource
options.rationale: Resource groups sit inside subscriptions.

options.text: Resource group, subscription, management group, resource
options.rationale: This inverts the hierarchy.

options.text: Management group, subscription, resource group, resource
options.rationale: This is the correct hierarchy.

questions.explanation: Management groups contain subscriptions; subscriptions contain resource groups; resource groups contain resources.
questions.concept_note: Management group > subscription > resource group > resource.

questions.stem: You delete a resource group that contains several resources. What happens to those resources?

options.text: They are all deleted with the resource group
options.rationale: Deleting a resource group deletes all resources it contains.
Resources cannot exist without a resource group.

options.text: They move to a default resource group
options.rationale: Azure has no automatic default group move.

options.text: The whole subscription is deleted too
options.rationale: Deletion cascades downward, not to the subscription.

questions.explanation: A resource group is a lifecycle container: deleting it deletes everything inside it. Use resource locks to prevent accidents.
questions.concept_note: Deleting a resource group deletes its resources.

questions.stem: You want to run small pieces of code in response to events and pay only per execution. Which Azure service fits?

options.rationale: VMs run continuously and you manage the OS.
Azure Functions is serverless and event-driven, billed per execution.
AKS orchestrates containers; it is not per-execution code.
App Service hosts always-on web apps.

questions.explanation: Azure Functions runs code triggered by events without managing servers, billed by usage.
questions.concept_note: Functions = serverless, event-driven, per-execution billing.

questions.stem: You need to run a single containerised app on demand without provisioning VMs or managing a Kubernetes cluster. Which service fits?

options.rationale: You would manage the VM and container runtime.
AKS requires a managed cluster for orchestration.
ACI runs containers on demand without managing VMs or orchestration.
AVD delivers virtual desktops and apps to users.

questions.explanation: Azure Container Instances is the simplest way to run a container in Azure without managing servers.
questions.concept_note: ACI = single containers on demand. AKS = orchestration at scale.

questions.stem: Which Azure Storage redundancy option copies data synchronously across three availability zones in the primary region?

options.rationale: LRS keeps three copies in a single datacenter.
GRS replicates asynchronously to a secondary region.
Access tiers affect cost and retrieval speed, not redundancy.
ZRS replicates synchronously across three availability zones.

questions.explanation: ZRS protects against a datacenter failure within the region by spreading copies across zones.
questions.concept_note: LRS = one datacenter. ZRS = three zones. GRS = adds a secondary region.

questions.stem: Which Azure Storage service is designed for large amounts of unstructured object data, such as images and videos?

options.rationale: Blob storage stores unstructured objects at scale.
Azure Files provides file shares.
Table storage holds NoSQL structured data.
Queue storage holds messages.

questions.explanation: Blob storage is the object store for unstructured data such as media, backups, and documents.
questions.concept_note: Blob = objects. Files = file shares. Table = NoSQL. Queue = messages.

questions.stem: A company needs a private, dedicated connection from its datacenter to Azure that does not travel over the public internet. What should it use?

options.rationale: VPN Gateway uses encrypted tunnels over the public internet.
ExpressRoute provides private connectivity to Azure.
Bastion provides secure RDP/SSH to VMs.
Peering connects Azure virtual networks.

questions.explanation: ExpressRoute extends on-premises networks into Azure over a private connection supplied by a connectivity provider.
questions.concept_note: ExpressRoute = private connection. VPN Gateway = encrypted over the internet.

questions.stem: You need allow/deny rules based on source, destination, port, and protocol, applied to a subnet or network interface. What should you use?

options.rationale: Load Balancer distributes traffic.
Azure Firewall is a centralised managed service, not subnet/NIC-level rules.
NSGs apply allow/deny rules to subnets and network interfaces.
Azure DNS resolves names.

questions.explanation: A network security group filters inbound and outbound traffic for Azure resources in a virtual network using security rules.
questions.concept_note: NSG = rules on subnet or NIC. Azure Firewall = centralised, managed. Load Balancer = distributes.

questions.stem: A legacy app in Azure needs LDAP, Kerberos, and domain join, and the team does not want to deploy domain controllers. What should it use?

options.rationale: Entra ID does not provide LDAP, Kerberos, or domain join.
Conditional Access enforces sign-in controls.
RBAC grants permissions on Azure resources.
Domain Services provides managed domain services such as LDAP, Kerberos, and domain join.

questions.explanation: Microsoft Entra Domain Services offers managed domain services compatible with Active Directory, without running your own domain controllers.
questions.concept_note: Entra ID = cloud identity. Entra Domain Services = managed AD DS-style services.

questions.stem: A user signs in with a password and a multifactor prompt to prove who they are. What is this process called?

options.rationale: Authentication verifies identity.
Authorization decides what an identity can access.
SSO lets one sign-in access multiple apps.
Role assignment grants permissions after identity is established.

questions.explanation: Authentication proves identity; authorization determines permitted actions afterwards.
questions.concept_note: Authentication = who you are. Authorization = what you can do.

questions.stem: You want to require multifactor authentication when users sign in from outside the corporate network. Which feature should you use?

options.rationale: RBAC governs what authenticated users can do.
Conditional Access evaluates signals such as location and enforces controls such as MFA.
Policy governs resource configuration.
Defender for Cloud assesses security posture.

questions.explanation: Conditional Access applies policies at sign-in using signals (user, location, device, risk) and enforces controls like MFA or blocking access.
questions.concept_note: Conditional Access = sign-in policy engine (signals, then controls).

questions.stem: You must stop anyone from deploying virtual machines outside approved Azure regions. What should you use?

options.rationale: RBAC controls who can act, not which configurations are allowed.
Locks block changes or deletion of existing resources.
Azure Policy can deny deployments that violate rules such as allowed locations.
Cost Management analyses spend; it does not block deployments.

questions.explanation: Azure Policy evaluates resource properties and can deny or audit non-compliant deployments. An authorised user with RBAC could otherwise still deploy to any region.
questions.concept_note: Policy = what is allowed. RBAC = who is allowed.

questions.stem: A production storage account must not be deleted by mistake, even by users with Owner permissions. What should you apply?

options.rationale: Policy does not prevent deletion of existing resources.
Tags are metadata and do not enforce anything.

options.text: The Reader role for everyone on the subscription
options.rationale: This removes needed access and is not the targeted control.
Locks override user permissions, including Owner.

questions.explanation: A CanNotDelete lock prevents deletion until the lock is removed, regardless of the user's role.
questions.concept_note: Resource locks: CanNotDelete and ReadOnly; they override RBAC permissions.

questions.stem: You assign a role to a user at the subscription scope. Which statement is correct?

options.text: It is inherited by all resource groups and resources in the subscription
options.rationale: RBAC permissions flow down the scope hierarchy.

options.text: It applies only to the subscription object itself
options.rationale: Permissions are inherited by child scopes.

options.text: It applies only to resources created after the assignment
options.rationale: It covers existing and future resources.

options.text: It applies only to resource groups, not individual resources
options.rationale: Resources inherit too.

questions.explanation: RBAC assignments are inherited by child scopes, so a role at subscription scope applies to everything beneath it.
questions.concept_note: Scope hierarchy: management group > subscription > resource group > resource; permissions inherit downward.

questions.stem: You want to estimate the monthly cost of new Azure resources before deploying them. Which tool should you use?

options.rationale: The TCO calculator compares on-premises costs with Azure.
The Pricing calculator estimates the cost of Azure services you configure.
Cost Management analyses actual spend.
Advisor gives recommendations on existing resources.

questions.explanation: Use the Pricing calculator to estimate costs of planned Azure services; use the TCO calculator for on-premises versus Azure comparisons.
questions.concept_note: Pricing calculator = estimate Azure cost. TCO = on-prem versus Azure. Cost Management = analyse actual spend.

questions.stem: A company runs VMs continuously with predictable demand. Which option can reduce their cost?

options.rationale: Locks protect resources and have no pricing effect.
Tags help report costs but do not reduce them.
Reservations give discounts for committing to steady usage.
Management groups organise governance and do not discount prices.

questions.explanation: Azure Reservations lower cost for predictable, long-running workloads in exchange for a one- or three-year commitment.
questions.concept_note: Reservations = commit for discount. Tags = allocation/reporting only.

questions.stem: An application depends on two services whose SLAs are 99.9% and 99.95%. Without added redundancy, what is the approximate composite SLA?

options.rationale: The composite cannot exceed the lowest individual SLA.
SLAs are multiplied, not averaged.
Combining dependencies lowers availability.

questions.explanation: Composite SLA = product of the individual SLAs: 0.999 × 0.9995 ≈ 0.9985 (about 99.85%).
questions.concept_note: Dependent services: multiply SLAs. Redundant paths can raise availability.

questions.stem: You want alerts about Azure platform incidents and planned maintenance that affect your resources. Which service should you use?

options.rationale: Service Health reports Azure outages and planned maintenance affecting you.
Monitor collects metrics and logs from your resources.
Advisor provides optimisation recommendations.
Defender for Cloud assesses security posture.

questions.explanation: Azure Service Health tracks Azure service issues and planned maintenance relevant to your subscriptions and regions.
questions.concept_note: Service Health = Azure platform incidents. Monitor = your telemetry. Advisor = recommendations.

questions.stem: Which service continuously assesses security posture and provides threat protection for workloads in Azure, on-premises, and other clouds?

options.rationale: Entra ID is an identity service.
Defender for Cloud provides security posture management and threat protection.
Advisor gives recommendations across reliability, cost, and more, but is not threat protection.
Policy enforces configuration standards.

questions.explanation: Microsoft Defender for Cloud assesses security posture and protects workloads across Azure, hybrid, and multicloud environments.
questions.concept_note: Defender for Cloud = posture management and workload protection.

questions.stem: Which option lets you manage Azure resources from a browser-based command line that is already authenticated, without installing tools locally?

options.rationale: The portal is a graphical interface.

options.text: Azure PowerShell installed on your computer
options.rationale: A local install requires setup on your machine.
Cloud Shell is a browser-based, pre-authenticated shell supporting Azure CLI and PowerShell.
ARM templates declare resources; they are not a shell.

questions.explanation: Azure Cloud Shell provides an authenticated command-line environment in the browser or portal.
questions.concept_note: Cloud Shell = browser-based shell (Bash or PowerShell), no local install.

questions.stem: A team wants to deploy identical Azure environments repeatably from declarative definitions. Which approach fits?

options.text: Manually creating resources in the Azure portal
options.rationale: Manual steps are not repeatable or declarative.
Arc extends Azure management to non-Azure resources.
Cloud Shell runs commands; it is not a declarative definition.
These declare resources and deploy them consistently.

questions.explanation: ARM templates and Bicep describe desired state declaratively so deployments are repeatable and consistent.
questions.concept_note: Infrastructure as code: ARM templates, Bicep.
